939.title: Expelled
939.hook: England expels its Jews, the start of a long line of expulsions
939.howItsDone: Jews remember past expulsions in study, in memorial prayers and on fast days such as Tisha B'Av, and some Jewish communities support refugees in memory of their own history.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the blood libels: a lie from Norwich that kept traveling. Your line was lies kill. Did a rumor stop with you? Today a new week begins, in the same country, with an order from the king. Day nine hundred thirty-nine.

In the middle of London there is a street called Old Jewry. People walk down it to work every day, past banks and offices. The name is older than any of the buildings. It marks where a Jewish neighborhood once stood: homes, a synagogue, a place where children learned their letters. Then one summer a royal order went out across England, and by the autumn those homes were empty. Today, one word for what happened to them.
screen: `A LONDON STREET CALLED OLD JEWRY.` → `A ROYAL ORDER.` → `EMPTY HOMES BY AUTUMN.`

segments.voice: The king was Edward the First. His order told every Jew in England to leave the kingdom by the feast of All Saints, and said that any who stayed after that would face death. They could take money and goods they could carry. Their houses, their debts owed to them and their synagogues passed to the crown. Some families crossed to France and other lands. Some, tradition says, did not survive the crossing. The order came at the end of a long squeeze. English Jews had been taxed again and again by the crown, restricted in the work they could do, and hit by the false stories we heard yesterday. By the time of the order, the community was far poorer than it had been. Expelled is a hard word. It doesn't mean moved, or migrated. It means pushed out, with a deadline, by people with the power to enforce it. And England's order was not the last. Other kingdoms and cities would issue their own over the following centuries, and in the coming days we will meet some of them. The Torah knows the experience from the inside. Its story keeps returning to leaving: Abraham told to go from his father's house, a people walking out of Egypt. And it turns that memory into a rule about others. In Exodus: "a stranger shalt thou not oppress; for ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." A people that remembers being pushed out is asked to remember it every time someone else arrives at the door.
screen: `EDWARD THE FIRST'S ORDER.` · `LEAVE BY ALL SAINTS.` · `A LONG SQUEEZE BEFORE.` · then, large: `YE KNOW THE HEART OF A STRANGER.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: think of those forced to leave home. Sit still and let your breath slow. Picture your own front door, and everything behind it you'd want to take. Now imagine being told you have a few months, and only what you can carry. Let that settle for a moment. Then widen the picture to the people, then and now, who have stood at that door for real. Hold them in mind, without needing to say anything. If you pray, you can remember them in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Expelled. Pushed out of a country by order, with a deadline: the fate of England's Jews under Edward the First, and of other communities after them. Today's word.
Your line: pushed out, with a deadline. Today, look up the story of one place near you whose name remembers people who are no longer there. Day nine hundred thirty-nine.

what a scholar hears: the order came after years of heavy royal taxation; the Torah's answer to such memory is 'ye know the heart of a stranger' (Exodus 23:9).

940.title: The Black Death (1348)
940.hook: Jews are blamed for the plague and whole communities murdered
940.howItsDone: On Yom Kippur, Jews read the Torah's account of the two goats in the synagogue service and confess their own wrongs aloud, together, in the first person plural.

segments.voice: Yesterday, expelled: a street in London that still remembers. Your line was pushed out, with a deadline. Did you find a place name with a story? Today, a sickness, and the blame that followed it. Day nine hundred forty.

A sickness moves along the trade routes into Europe. It arrives in a town, and within days families are burying their own. Nobody understands how it spreads. Doctors argue about bad air and the stars. Priests call for prayer and processions. And in town after town, a rumor arrives as well, sometimes before the sickness itself: the Jews are poisoning the wells. Today, the Black Death, and what fear did with that rumor.
screen: `A SICKNESS ON THE TRADE ROUTES.` → `NOBODY KNOWS HOW IT SPREADS.` → `A RUMOR ARRIVES TOO.`

segments.voice: The plague killed rich and poor, Christian and Jew. But the rumor needed someone to blame. In some places, Jews were arrested and tortured until they confessed to poisoning, and those forced confessions were copied and sent on to other towns as proof. And the killing spread. In parts of the German lands, in Switzerland, in Alsace, whole communities were murdered, often burned, sometimes before the plague had even reached the town. Some voices pushed back. Pope Clement the Sixth issued a bull that answered the rumor directly. He pointed out that Jews were dying of the plague like everyone else, and that it was raging in places where no Jews lived at all. He ordered that Jews not be harmed. In town after town, the killing went on anyway. Our line today borrows a word from the Day of Atonement, though the Torah means something very different by it. In Leviticus the high priest takes two goats. One is offered. Over the other he lays his hands and confesses the sins of the people, and then the goat is sent off into the wilderness. The Hebrew says it goes to Azazel. The King James Bible gives the English word, saying the goat is kept alive "to let him go for a scapegoat into the wilderness." Notice what the ritual does. The priest names the people's own wrongs, out loud, before the goat goes. At the center of the rite is taking responsibility. The plague years ran it backward: a frightened crowd invented guilt and laid it on the people next door. The goat carried away sins the people had confessed as their own. The Jews of those towns were blamed for sins nobody had committed.
screen: `A RUMOR NEEDS SOMEONE TO BLAME.` · `CLEMENT THE SIXTH ANSWERS IT.` · `TWO GOATS ON THE DAY OF ATONEMENT.` · then, large: `THE PEOPLE NAME THEIR OWN SINS.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: refuse to scapegoat anyone. Let your shoulders drop and your breath slow. Think of something going wrong right now: at work, at home, in the news. Notice if your mind has already chosen someone to blame, especially someone who isn't in the room. Gently set that name down. Ask instead: what part of this is simply hard, and what part is mine? Rest with that question. The bell holds the time.
Azazel. Where the Torah's scapegoat is sent in Leviticus, the image behind a plague-year rumor that blamed Jews for the Black Death. Today's word.
Your line: no scapegoats. Today, when something goes wrong and a name comes to mind, check whether it's the cause or just the easiest target. Day nine hundred forty.

941.title: Poland
941.hook: Polish rulers invite Jews east, and a great center grows
941.howItsDone: Jewish tradition values hachnasat orchim, welcoming guests, and some communities make a point of inviting newcomers to a Shabbat meal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Black Death, and two goats in Leviticus. Your line was no scapegoats. Did you catch yourself reaching for an easy target? Today the road turns east, toward a door that opened. Day nine hundred forty-one.

In a story Jews told about how they came to Poland, a group of refugees, tired of being driven from town to town in the west, walks east into a forest. They don't know where they are or whether they'll be allowed to stay. And on the trees, or on a slip of paper falling from the sky, depending on who tells it, they find two Hebrew words: po lin. Here, rest. Here, spend the night. So they stayed, and they called the land Polin. Today, the land behind the legend.
screen: `REFUGEES IN AN EASTERN FOREST.` → `TWO HEBREW WORDS: PO LIN.` → `HERE, REST.`

segments.voice: The legend is wordplay. Polin is the Hebrew name for Poland, and it sounds like po lin, here lodge. It is a folk story, not a historian's account of the name. But it holds something real: for Jews leaving the violence we've followed this week, Poland looked like a place to rest. Behind the legend there are documents. A Polish duke, Bolesław the Pious, issued a charter for the Jews of his lands, known as the Statute of Kalisz. Later Polish kings confirmed and widened it. The charter protected Jewish lives and property, let Jews trade, and allowed them to run their own courts and synagogues. It even dealt with the lie from Norwich we met a few days ago. It said that Jews were not to be accused of using Christian blood, and that anyone who made such a charge without proof would be punished. Why invite them? The rulers wanted towns, trade and people who could run markets and keep accounts. The welcome was practical, and it was never perfect. There would be riots and hard years in Poland too. But over time, communities grew, schools grew, and Poland became a home where Jewish learning flourished. An old instruction fits this moment. When the prophet Jeremiah wrote to exiles in Babylon, he told them to build houses, plant gardens, and "seek the peace of the city" where they had been sent, because their peace was bound up with its peace. In Poland, for centuries, many Jews built houses, planted, and stayed.
screen: `PO LIN: HERE, REST.` · `THE STATUTE OF KALISZ.` · `A PRACTICAL WELCOME.` · then, large: `SEEK THE PEACE OF THE CITY.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: welcome one newcomer. Sit comfortably and let your breathing slow. Think of someone new in your life: a coworker, a neighbor, a classmate, a family that just moved in, someone new at your synagogue, church or gym. Picture them a little unsure, still learning where things are. Now picture one small way to say, here, you can rest: a name remembered, a question asked, an invitation. Hold that picture. The bell holds the time.
Poland. Polin in Hebrew, read by legend as here, rest. A land whose rulers invited Jews in with a charter of protection, and where a great center of Jewish life grew. Today's word.
Your line: poland invites. Today, make the welcome you pictured real: one greeting, one name learned, one door held open. Day nine hundred forty-one.

942.title: Yiddish
942.hook: a language built from German, Hebrew and Slavic words, the everyday tongue of Ashkenaz
942.howItsDone: Yiddish is still the everyday language in some Hasidic homes, and in other Jewish families it lives on in words, songs, sayings and Yiddish classes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Poland: po lin, here, rest, and a charter that opened a door. Your line was poland invites. Did you welcome someone? Today, what people spoke once they were through that door. Day nine hundred forty-two.

Schlep. Kvetch. Mensch. Chutzpah. Some English speakers use these words without a second thought: carrying something heavy, complaining, a decent human being, a lot of nerve. Each one came into English from a single language, spoken in kitchens and markets and study halls across Ashkenazi Europe. A grandmother scolding, a peddler bargaining over the price of a coat, a child reciting a lesson, a love letter, a joke that only works in the original. For Ashkenazi Jews it was the sound of home. Today, the language itself.
screen: `SCHLEP, KVETCH, MENSCH.` → `KITCHENS AND MARKETS.` → `ONE LANGUAGE BEHIND THEM.`

segments.voice: In Yiddish, the word Yiddish simply means Jewish. It grew among the Jews of Ashkenaz, the German lands, and traveled east with them into Poland and beyond. Its backbone is German, but it is full of Hebrew and Aramaic words for the things of Jewish life, and it took in Slavic words as Jews settled further east. And it is written in Hebrew letters, right to left. Think about what that meant in daily life. A Jew in a Polish town lived with two Jewish languages. One was loshn koydesh, the holy tongue: Hebrew, and the Aramaic of the Talmud, for prayer, Torah and study. The other was mame loshn, the mother tongue: the language your mother sang to you in, the language of the market, the kitchen and the jokes. Our line today is mama loshen, an English spelling of that phrase. Yiddish also opened the texts to people who had not been taught Hebrew. One well-known book, the Tsene-rene, retold the Torah readings in Yiddish, full of stories and commentary, and tradition says women read it on Shabbat and passed it from mother to daughter. Yiddish was sometimes looked down on, even by Jews, as a mere jargon. But it is a full language, with its own grammar, its own songs, newspapers, theater and great writers. And it is not finished. Yiddish is still spoken today, in homes and in schools, and studied by people finding their way back to it. A mensch, by the way, means more than a person. It means someone decent, someone you can count on.
screen: `YIDDISH MEANS JEWISH.` · `GERMAN, HEBREW, SLAVIC.` · `HOLY TONGUE, MOTHER TONGUE.` · then, large: `A FULL LANGUAGE, STILL SPOKEN.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: learn one Yiddish word. Take mensch: a decent human being, someone you can rely on. Sit back and let your breath slow. Say the word to yourself, quietly. Then bring to mind someone you'd call a mensch: someone who showed up, kept their word, was kind when nobody was watching. Picture their face. Let the word and the face sit together. The bell holds the time.
Yiddish. The everyday language of Ashkenazi Jews, German at its core, full of Hebrew and Slavic words, written in Hebrew letters: the mother tongue beside the holy tongue. Today's word.
Your line: mama loshen. Today, tell the person you pictured that they're a mensch, in whatever words you have. Day nine hundred forty-two.

943.title: Glückel of Hameln
943.hook: a merchant widow writes her memoir in Yiddish for her children
943.howItsDone: Glückel's memoir is still read in Yiddish and in translation, and some Jewish families keep the custom of an ethical will, a letter of memories and values left for children.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yiddish: the mother tongue beside the holy tongue. Your line was mama loshen. Did you call someone a mensch? Today, a mother who wrote in that tongue, at night, for her children. Day nine hundred forty-three.

Hamburg, late at night. The house is quiet, the children asleep. A widow sits up with a pen because she cannot sleep. Her husband, her partner in business and in everything else, has died, and the long nights are the worst part. So she begins to write. Not a book of law, not a commentary. Her own life: her childhood, her marriage, the deals and journeys, the births and the deaths, the stories she wants her children to keep. Today, Glückel of Hameln.
screen: `A WIDOW AWAKE IN HAMBURG.` → `SHE CANNOT SLEEP.` → `SO SHE WRITES HER LIFE.`

segments.voice: Glückel wrote in Yiddish, and she tells us why she wrote. It was to ease her grief through the sleepless nights, and so that her children would know where they came from. She was not a scholar or a rabbi's daughter writing for the learned. She was a businesswoman. Her husband Chaim dealt in gold and jewels, and she worked beside him; he asked her advice, she says, on everything. After his death she ran the business herself, dealing with creditors, traveling to trade fairs, arranging her children's marriages. All of it goes into the memoir, alongside plague, debts, family quarrels and moments of deep faith. She fills it with moral stories too, and one of them sticks. A father bird has to carry his three chicks across a wide river. Halfway over, he asks the first: when I'm old, will you carry me like this? Yes, says the chick. The father drops it, saying it's a lie. The second chick says yes too, and goes the same way. The third says: I can't promise that. But I will carry my own children like this. That one the father carries safely to the other shore. Glückel tells it with a wry honesty. She doesn't ask her children to repay her. She asks them to pass it on. Why does her book matter here? Many of the voices in recent days have been rabbis and chroniclers. Glückel lets us hear a Jewish home from the inside, in the voice of the woman who ran it.
screen: `WRITTEN AT NIGHT, IN YIDDISH.` · `A BUSINESSWOMAN, NOT A SCHOLAR.` · `THE FATHER BIRD AND THREE CHICKS.` · then, large: `CARRY YOUR OWN CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: write down one memory. If you can, take a scrap of paper or open a note on your phone. Breathe slowly for a moment. Let one small scene from your family come up: a kitchen, a journey, something someone said once and you never forgot. Write it in two or three plain sentences, the way Glückel did, for someone who comes after you. Then sit with what you wrote. The bell holds the time.
Glückel. A Jewish businesswoman and widow in Hamburg who wrote her life story in Yiddish for her children, to ease her grief. Today's word.
Your line: a woman's memoir. Today, send the memory you wrote to one person who'd want it, or keep it somewhere you'll find it again. Day nine hundred forty-three.

944.title: The shtetl
944.hook: the small market towns of Eastern Europe
944.howItsDone: Some Ashkenazi Jewish families trace their roots to a particular shtetl, and some keep memorial books (yizkor books) that record its streets, families and customs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Glückel of Hameln, writing her life at night in Hamburg. Your line was a woman's memoir. Did you write your memory down? Today, the kind of place where other Jewish memories would one day be set. Day nine hundred forty-four.

Market day. Carts roll in from the villages before dawn: peasants with eggs, grain, a cow to sell. In the square, Jewish shopkeepers open their stalls and the bargaining starts, in Yiddish, in Polish, in Ukrainian, in whatever works. The street is mud in spring and dust in summer. Somewhere a tailor is at work, a water carrier sloshes past with two buckets, and from an open window comes the sing-song of boys reading Torah aloud. Today, the place where all of this happened at once.

Shtetl is the Yiddish word for a small town. It names the market towns of Eastern Europe, in the lands of Poland and beyond, where Jewish families lived beside Christian neighbors who came in to trade. A shtetl had a shape. The market square at its center. The synagogue, and next to it the study house, where men and boys read and argued over the Talmud. The mikveh, the ritual bath. The cemetery at the edge of town. Around them, wooden houses and the trades that kept everyone fed: tailors, cobblers, innkeepers, peddlers, teachers. Life was hard. Families were often poor, fires could take a street in a night, and a ruler's whim or a riot could turn everything over. But the week had a rhythm stronger than any of that. On Friday afternoon the shops closed, the bathhouse filled, the bread was baked, and when the candles were lit Shabbat came in, and for a day even the poorest home could feel like a palace. Writers in Yiddish loved the shtetl and teased it at the same time. Sholem Aleichem invented a town called Kasrilevke, poor and crowded and full of characters, and wrote about it with laughter and tenderness. Today we have the word, the stories and the photographs. What happened to the towns themselves, we will come to later in the year.
screen: `A LITTLE TOWN.` · `SQUARE, SYNAGOGUE, STUDY HOUSE.` · `HARD WEEKS, HOLY SHABBAT.` · then, large: `LOVED AND TEASED.`

Walk down that street slowly, and let it be quiet. The bell holds the time.
Shtetl. A small market town of Eastern Europe, Jewish at its heart: a square, a synagogue, a study house, mud, poverty and Shabbat candles. Today's word.
Your line: the little town. Today, ask someone older where their family came from, the town's name, if anyone remembers it, and write it down. Day nine hundred forty-four.

945.title: The Inquisition
945.hook: converts are watched and tried; some keep Judaism in secret
945.howItsDone: Jewish communities remember the anusim, the forced converts, in study and storytelling, and some descendants of conversos today are exploring and reclaiming their Jewish roots.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shtetl: mud, a market square, candles on Friday. Your line was the little town. Did you find a town's name in your family? Today, the end of the week, and candles of a very different kind, lit in secret, far to the west. Day nine hundred forty-five.

Friday evening in a Spanish city. A family that has been Christian on paper for years sits down to dinner. Before sunset the mother has changed the tablecloth and put on clean linen. Somewhere out of sight, perhaps inside a jar, perhaps in a cellar, a small lamp is burning. Nobody says why. Across the street, a neighbor notices the clean linen and the smokeless chimney on Saturday. That neighbor may soon be asked to tell what they saw. Today, the conversos, and the Inquisition that watched them.
screen: `FRIDAY IN A SPANISH CITY.` → `A LAMP IN A JAR.` → `A NEIGHBOR WATCHING.`

segments.voice: We return to Spain, where we left it with the riots. In those riots and the years that followed, Jews converted to Christianity, some under threat of death, some under pressure, some by their own choice. In Spanish they were called conversos, converts, or New Christians. Some became devoted Catholics. Some kept parts of Jewish life in secret. Others lived somewhere in between. Hebrew sources call those forced into baptism anusim, the ones who were compelled. Suspicion fell on conversos as a group. The Spanish Inquisition was a tribunal set up under the Spanish crown, with the pope's approval, to root out heresy among the baptized. That detail matters: it had authority over Christians, so in its early years its chief target was the converso, the Christian suspected of still being a Jew. The Inquisition published lists of signs to watch for: lighting candles on Friday night, changing into clean clothes for the Sabbath, refusing pork, fasting on the Day of Atonement, washing a body for burial in the Jewish way. Neighbors and servants were invited to come forward. Trials followed, with property seized, families shamed, and some of the accused burned. Sincere Christians were caught up too, because a family's past was enough to make it suspect. So what was hidden faith? Sometimes a few customs kept up without words. A grandmother's habit of lighting a candle out of sight. A prayer whispered in a mixture of languages. Tradition says some families kept such customs for generations, long after anyone remembered the reason. This week has followed Jews out of England, through the plague years, into Poland and its little towns, through Yiddish and Glückel's pages. It ends here, with faith kept behind a closed door.

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: honor hidden faith. Let your breath settle. Think of the people, in every age and every tradition, who have had to keep what they believed out of sight. Picture one of them: a mother in Spain changing the tablecloth on a Friday, someone keeping a fast at a work lunch without a word, a person reading scripture on a phone under a desk. You don't need words. Just keep them company for a moment. If you pray, you can remember them in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Converso. A Jew who became a Christian in Spain or Portugal, by force, pressure or choice, and who could be watched, accused and tried for keeping Jewish ways. Today's word.
Your line: hidden faith. Today, if you see someone keeping a quiet custom, a grace before eating, a fast, a head covering, give it room without comment. Day nine hundred forty-five.

myth: the Spanish Inquisition put unbaptized Jews on trial for being Jewish
it had authority over the baptized; its early chief target was the converso suspected of still being a Jew.
every converso secretly kept Judaism
some became devoted Catholics, some kept Jewish ways in secret, and others lived in between.
the Inquisition published lists of Jewish customs for neighbors to watch for
Friday candles, clean clothes for the Sabbath, refusing pork, fasting on the Day of Atonement.

fork.setup: you are a converso. it's Friday evening, and the Inquisition has published a list of signs to watch for. what does a family keeping hidden faith do?
options: light candles openly in the window.
keep a small lamp out of sight, perhaps in a jar or a cellar.
stop every custom at once.
fork.reveal: some kept customs quietly, out of sight, and tradition says some families kept them for generations.

original.note: Hebrew: anusim, the ones who were compelled, forced converts.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Inquisition persecuted Jews for being Jewish.
what it means: its authority was over the baptized, so in its early years it hunted conversos, Christians suspected of keeping Jewish ways in secret.
what a scholar hears: it published lists of signs, like Friday candles and clean Sabbath linen, and invited neighbors and servants to report them.
